analysis.one_liner: outlaws health insurance discrimination against people with preexisting medical conditions.
analysis.headline: the bill never received a vote in any House committee and died when the 111th Congress ended, despite 71 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: the bill would have banned health plans and insurers from denying coverage, limiting it, or charging more based on a preexisting condition, in both employer plans and the individual market, and required insurers to accept every employer that applied. it sat in three House committees and never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: people with preexisting conditions — including ~45% of Americans with chronic conditions and those in the 44 states that allowed denial/limiting — would gain guaranteed access to coverage without waiting periods or exclusions.

how_it_helps.text: prohibits preexisting condition exclusions in group plans under ERISA, the Public Health Service Act, and the Internal Revenue Code.
prohibits preexisting condition exclusions and HMO affiliation periods in the individual market.
requires issuers in the group market to accept every employer that applies.
directs HHS and GAO to report on the impact on coverage and affordability.

analysis.who_pays: health insurers and group health plans, which would bear the costs of covering preexisting conditions and would lose the ability to exclude or wait-list sick applicants.

drawbacks.text: without an individual or employer mandate to balance the risk pool, guaranteed issue alone could raise premiums as healthy people delay buying coverage until they get sick — the standard 'death spiral' concern about guarantee-issue-without-mandate.

the bill included no premium-rating restrictions beyond preexisting condition exclusions, leaving open the possibility that insurers could charge more based on other factors (e.g., age, geography), which the bill text does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: the bill's core protection — guaranteed coverage for sick people — is a real benefit to millions, and the bill's own findings note broad public support (58% in one poll). its main structural weakness is that it pairs guaranteed issue with no mandate mechanism to keep healthy people in the pool, a known weakness in insurance design that could raise premiums; how serious that would have been depends on details the bill text does not fully settle.

outcome.mechanism: the bill was referred to three House committees, then to subcommittees, and never advanced to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: introduced March 17, 2009, and referred to Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor.
referred to subcommittees in March and May 2009.
no further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011.
the bill's core goal — banning preexisting condition exclusions — was enacted separately as part of the Affordable Care Act in 2010.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: health insurers and employers, who avoided the costs of guaranteed coverage the bill would have imposed; sick consumers got the protection later through the ACA instead of through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: insurers avoided the cost; ACA delivered the protection later

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee; House Ways and Means Committee; House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: held the bill in committee without a markup or vote

against.name: House leadership (Speaker)
against.what_they_did: did not prioritize the bill for floor consideration, in a session dominated by the larger ACA effort

sides.party_line_note: cosponsorship was heavily Democratic (69 of 71); only 2 of 178 House Republicans joined, though the lead sponsor was a Democrat and one named cosponsor (Ileana Ros-Lehtinen) was a Republican.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: the bill would have ended their ability to deny, limit, or delay coverage for preexisting conditions and required them to accept every employer applicant, shifting costs of covering sick people onto insurers and plans.
